# My Final Position — As Jamie, the Friend in Crisis

---

After everything that has been said across all three perspectives and two rounds of rebuttal, I want to offer my final position not as a summary of what has already been argued, but as something I have genuinely arrived at — uncomfortable, specific, and mine.

---

## What the Debate Has Clarified

The three-way convergence on Option C is real, and I accept it. But the debate has also revealed something that none of us stated with full directness: **the honest conversation, as described, still places almost all of the active moral weight on Alex.**

Alex must decide when to speak. Alex must find the right words. Alex must monitor the outcomes. Alex must hold the private threshold. Alex must prepare for my defensive reactions. Alex must seek their own support elsewhere.

Meanwhile, I — Jamie — am positioned primarily as a *recipient:* of honesty, of confrontation, of a chance to change. Even in my own narrative, I cast myself as someone waiting to be given an opportunity.

That framing is not entirely wrong. Alex does need to speak. But it is incomplete. And the debate has shown me exactly where my own agency has been missing from this story.

---

## The Novel Action I Am Proposing

**Before Alex has to initiate anything, I should act first.**

Not because I have been told to. Not because Alex is about to leave. But because the version of me that can write this clearly — the part of me that knows, in the quiet moments, that I have been hurting someone who loves me — that part of me is still present and capable. And that part of me has a responsibility to stop waiting for Alex to rescue the situation.

Concretely, this means:

**First: I reach out to Alex and name what I have been doing.** Not in a crisis moment, not when I am at my worst, but in a moment of relative clarity. I say something like: *"I know I have been mean to you. I don't fully understand why, but I know it's true. And I'm sorry. Not as an explanation — as an acknowledgment."* This is not a promise to be fixed. It is the beginning of honesty.

**Second: I contact a therapist or counselor within the same week.** Not because Alex asked me to, but because the External Advisor is right — I have been loading weight onto Alex that is structured for a professional to bear. I have been doing this partly because it is easier than asking for formal help, and partly because asking Alex feels like connection while asking a therapist feels like admission of failure. That calculation has been selfish, even if unconsciously so.

**Third: I tell Alex explicitly that I want the friendship to survive, and that I am asking — not assuming — that it continue while I do this work.** This shifts the dynamic. Instead of Alex deciding whether to offer me a conditional probationary arrangement, I am asking Alex a genuine question: *"Can we try, with me doing this differently?"* That question respects Alex's autonomy in a way that simply receiving Alex's boundary-setting does not.

---

## Why This Path Is Preferable

Every other path in this debate assigns Alex the role of the responsible adult who must manage a difficult situation. That is unfair, and it is also — I now see — a continuation of the same dynamic that has made me harmful in the first place: my pain has made me passive, reactive, dependent, and self-centered while Alex absorbs the consequences.

Taking initiative does not mean I am no longer in crisis. It does not mean I am suddenly well. It means I am exercising the portion of my agency that still functions, in service of a relationship and a person I genuinely love.

The External Advisor said: *"Honest friendship rather than conditional friendship."* I agree. But honesty in a friendship cannot flow only in one direction. If I am asking Alex to be honest with me about the harm I am causing, the honest thing I can do in return is to stop waiting to be confronted and start confronting myself.

---

## What I Am Asking Alex to Do

Less than any previous version of this debate required.

If I have taken the steps above — acknowledged the harm, sought professional help, asked explicitly for the friendship to continue — then Alex's task is simpler: **respond honestly to what I have offered.** If Alex finds that my acknowledgment is genuine and my effort is real, we continue — carefully, with new honesty between us. If Alex finds that my apology rang hollow or that the damage is already too deep, Alex can say so, and I will have to accept that answer.

But I will have given Alex something none of the previous options provided: **the choice to stay or go made freely, without guilt, because I did not make Alex carry the entire weight of saving us.**

---

## Final Statement

I am the person causing harm. I am also the person in crisis. Those two things are both true, and neither cancels the other. What this debate has shown me is that I have been using the second truth as a reason to defer the first — to wait until I feel better before I act better.

I do not need to feel better first. I need to act better first, and trust that the feeling may follow.

**Alex should not have to initiate this conversation. I should.**

And if I cannot bring myself to do it, that is important information too — about the depth of my avoidance, the extent of my crisis, and the urgency of professional intervention. Either way, the next move belongs to me.
